column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we follow Alexander the Great into Asia, to his first two great battles against the Persian Empire: at the river Gran-eye-kus in 334 BCE, and at Issus a year and a half later. Alexander was twenty-one years old when he crossed into Asia. His opponent at Issus was Darius the Third, the Great King of Persia, who ruled a vast empire stretching across many peoples and lands. Almost everything we know comes from writers who lived centuries later, and most of what they used came from Alexander's side. We will tell you what they say, where they disagree, and what is still not known.

Gran-eye-kus and issus. In the spring of 334 BCE, Alexander, king of Macedon, crossed from Europe into Asia with an army of Macedonians, Greek allies and other troops. Near the river Gran-eye-kus, the Persian governors of the region met him with their cavalry and with Greek soldiers who served Persia. Alexander won. In the autumn of 333 BCE, at Issus, on the coast where Anatolia meets Syria, he met the Great King himself, Darius the Third, and won again. Darius escaped. His family was captured. Neither battle ended the Persian Empire. Two years after Issus, Alexander defeated Darius again at Gaw-ga-mee-la. Darius remained at large until 330 BCE.

Two kingdoms. Macedon was a kingdom in the north of Greece. Alexander's father, Philip the Second, made it the strongest power in the Greek world. The Persian Empire, ruled by the A-kee-meh-nid kings, stretched from the Aegean Sea to India and Egypt. It was made of many peoples, governed by provincial governors called Say-traps. Its king was called the Great King. In 336 BCE, Darius the Third came to the throne. Many Greeks lived inside the Persian Empire, in the cities of the Anatolian coast. Many Greek soldiers served the Great King for pay.

Why the war?. After defeating a Greek coalition at Ker-o-nee-a in 338 BCE, Philip formed an alliance of Greek states under Macedonian leadership, and prepared a war against Persia. The war was presented as revenge for the Persian invasions of Greece more than a century before. That was its public justification. Not every Greek shared it. Philip sent an advance force into Asia under his general Par-mee-nee-on. Then, in 336 BCE, Philip was murdered. Who else may have been behind it is still debated. Alexander, aged twenty, became king.

The writers. Our main source is Arrian, who wrote in Greek about four hundred and fifty years later. He used the lost histories of two men who served with Alexander: Ptolemy and A-ris-tob-yoo-lus. We also have Dye-o-dor-us, Plutarch, Kur-shus and Justin, and the criticisms of Po-lib-ee-us. They often disagree, about what happened, in what order, and above all about numbers. Most surviving narratives were written in Greek or Latin after the campaign, and draw on accounts from Alexander's side. No equivalent Persian history of these battles survives. Earlier does not always mean more accurate, and later does not always mean worthless.

The armies. Alexander's army was built around the phalanx: rows of infantry armed with long pikes called Sa-ris-az. Beside them fought the Hy-pas-pists, the king's guard infantry. His striking force was the cavalry: the Companions, Macedonian nobles, and alongside them the horsemen of Thes-a-lee. Light troops, like the Ag-ree-ay-nee-an javelin-men, guarded the flanks. The Persian army was the army of an empire: Persian and Iranian noble cavalry, infantry and archers from many peoples, and many thousands of Greek mercenaries. Ancient writers give widely different army and casualty figures. The enormous Persian totals cannot be treated as reliable headcounts, and the actual strengths and losses remain uncertain.

How this page tells it. After each line, a tag tells you who says it. Where the writers disagree, we say so. The maps are paintings made for this page over real elevation data. Where a battlefield's exact place is uncertain, the map says so. The positions and movements of the soldiers are our own reconstruction, following Arrian.

Thebes. Before leaving for Asia, Alexander campaigned north of Macedon, among the Try-bal-ee-anz and other peoples. A false report that he had been killed set off a revolt at Thebes. Alexander marched south at speed. Thebes was taken and destroyed, and many of its people were enslaved. Athens was spared. The destruction of Thebes frightened the other Greek cities. Alexander left his general An-tip-a-ter in charge of Europe.

Into Asia. In the spring of 334 BCE, Par-mee-nee-on took the main army across the Hel-es-pont, the narrow strait between Europe and Asia, from Ses-tos to A-by-dos. Alexander crossed separately, toward the coast of Troy. Dye-o-dor-us says he threw a spear into the soil of Asia as he landed, a claim to the land. At Troy, Alexander honoured the tomb of Achilles, the hero of the Iliad, and visited the sanctuary of Athena. His army numbered some tens of thousands. The ancient writers' counts, on the screen, do not agree exactly.

The council at Zeh-lye-a. The Persian governors of the region gathered their forces at Zeh-lye-a. Memnon of Rhodes, a Greek commander in Persian service, advised them not to fight: to burn the crops and farms, so that Alexander's army would run out of food. Ar-sy-teez, the Say-trap of the region, refused to burn the land of the people he governed. Arrian says the Persian commanders also distrusted Memnon. That is Arrian's explanation; no Persian record of the council survives. They decided to fight at a river.

The river. The Persians took up position on the far bank of the river Gran-eye-kus, today usually identified as the Biga Çayı in north-western Turkey. In Arrian's account, the Persian cavalry lined the bank, with the Greek mercenary infantry behind them. Exactly where they stood is uncertain. Reyhan Kur-peh's 2025 survey proposes a crossing north of the modern town of Biga; its exact location is still debated.

Two stories. Here the ancient writers tell two different stories, and they cannot both be true. In Arrian and Plutarch, Par-mee-nee-on advised waiting until morning, and Alexander refused, and attacked across the river at once. In Dye-o-dor-us, the army crossed at dawn, and formed up before the Persians could stop it. This page follows Arrian's version. The historians Bad-ee-an and Devine also use his account as their main basis.

The first attack. In Arrian's account, Alexander sent a first group across ahead of his main charge: horsemen and light infantry, with a squadron of Companions led by Ptolemy, son of Philip. They met fierce resistance at the bank. As the survivors fell back toward him, Alexander was already approaching with the right wing.

The fight at the bank. Arrian describes a fight of horsemen at the water's edge, at close quarters, with lances and swords. Alexander struck down Mith-rih-day-teez, a son-in-law of Darius. A Persian noble, Roy-sa-seez, struck Alexander's helmet. As Spith-rih-day-teez, a Say-trap, raised his sword against the king, Alexander's officer Kly-tus, called the Black, struck his sword arm and stopped the blow. Plutarch and Dye-o-dor-us tell this fight differently, with other names and other blows. We follow Arrian, and do not combine them.

The mercenaries. The Persian cavalry gave way and withdrew. Behind them, the Greek mercenaries remained in position. Plutarch says the mercenaries asked for terms, but Alexander attacked them. Alexander surrounded them with infantry and cavalry. Arrian says most were killed, and about two thousand were taken prisoner. The prisoners were sent to Macedonia to work the land as forced labourers. Arrian's explanation: the Greek alliance had forbidden Greeks to fight for Persia.

After the Gran-eye-kus. Several Persian commanders were killed. Ar-sy-teez escaped, and Arrian says he later killed himself. Alexander sent three hundred Persian suits of armour to the goddess Athena at Athens, says Arrian; Plutarch speaks of shields. Both say the dedication left out the Spartans, who had not joined the war. The ancient figures for the losses, on screen, differ widely. The victory opened western Anatolia to Alexander. It did not destroy the Persian Empire.

Sardis and Ephesus. The people of Sardis, the old capital of Lydia, submitted, and its Persian commander, Mith-ree-neez, surrendered the citadel. At Ephesus, Alexander brought back exiles and replaced the ruling few with a democracy. Arrian says he stopped the killing of political opponents there. The Greek cities were divided. Some citizens supported Persia, others Alexander.

Miletus and the fleet. Miletus resisted. Alexander's fleet secured the anchorage at Lah-dee, off the harbour, before the larger Persian fleet arrived. Par-mee-nee-on urged a sea battle; Alexander refused. His siege engines broke the walls, and the city fell. Then Alexander sent most of his fleet home. Arrian says it was too costly, and that he planned to defeat the Persian navy by taking its harbours on land. Dye-o-dor-us gives cost as one reason, and also reports that some said it was to leave his army no way of escape.

Hal-ih-kar-nas-us and Ay-da. At Hal-ih-kar-nas-us, Memnon and the Persian commander Or-on-tob-a-teez organised a strong defence, with sorties against the siege engines. The defenders set fires and withdrew into the city's strongholds. Then, according to Arrian, Alexander ordered the city demolished. Ay-da, a princess of the ruling family of Caria who had been pushed out of power, offered Alexander her stronghold of A-lin-da and adopted him as her son. He entrusted Caria to her.

The winter march. Alexander sent the soldiers who had recently married home to Macedonia for the winter. He marched along the southern coast, through Lish-a and Pam-fil-ee-a, where cities submitted. At Mount Climax the road ran along the shore. Some accounts said the sea drew back for him. Plutarch criticised those embellished stories. In the spring, the army gathered again at Gor-dee-um, in the heart of Anatolia.

A-ris-tob-yoo-lus says he pulled out the pin that held the yoke. Arrian says he cannot say for certain how it was done. Meanwhile, Memnon led the Persian fleet into the Aegean. He took Ky-os and most of Lesbos, and then died of illness while besieging Mit-ih-lee-nee. The Persian navy fought on under other commanders. The war was not only a war on land.

Tarsus. Alexander crossed the Taurus mountains by the narrow pass called the Sih-lish-an Gates, and hurried to Tarsus before its Persian governor could burn it. At Tarsus he fell dangerously ill. A-ris-tob-yoo-lus blamed exhaustion; other writers blamed bathing in the cold river Sid-nus. His doctor, Philip of Ak-ar-nay-nee-a, treated him. The writers tell of a letter accusing the doctor of a plot. It is an episode reported by the ancient writers; its details cannot be independently confirmed.

He waited at So-koy, on open ground east of the Amanus mountains, where his cavalry could fight best. Arrian says a Macedonian exile in his service, A-min-tas, advised him to stay there. Darius moved. The ancient writers blame flattering courtiers; that is their explanation, not a Persian record.

Then he turned his army round, and marched back north.

Darius escaped; his family was captured. Neither battle ended the Persian Empire. How the Gran-eye-kus began: an attack at once, in Arrian; a dawn crossing, in Dye-o-dor-us. Who struck whom in the fight at the bank. The sizes of the armies and the numbers killed: the Persian totals are far too large to be counts. Where exactly the two battles were fought. No Persian history of these battles survives. We see Darius almost only through Greek and Roman eyes.

Darius leaves the field. Alexander's victorious right wing turned against the Greek mercenaries, helping the hard-pressed Macedonian centre. Arrian says Darius fled, first in his chariot, then on horseback when the ground grew rough. Dye-o-dor-us tells of fierce fighting around the royal chariot. A personal duel between the two kings is not established. Plutarch says Alexander was wounded in the thigh. The historian Ernst Bad-ee-an suggests that Darius escaped to preserve his kingdom's chance of resistance. That is a modern interpretation.

The rout. With the king gone, the Persian army broke. Many died in the pursuit and the crush in the narrow passes. The ancient figures for the dead, on screen, are very large and very different. They cannot be treated as counts.

The royal family. The Persian camp was taken. Among the captives were Darius's mother, Sis-ee-gam-bis, his wife, Sta-ty-ra, his daughters and his young son. The writers say Alexander promised them protection and their royal rank. They remained captives. Other people taken in the camp did not share their privileged treatment. A famous story says Sis-ee-gam-bis bowed first to Alexander's friend Heh-fees-tee-on, mistaking him for the king. Arrian tells it only as a story he cannot vouch for.

Damascus and the survivors. Par-mee-nee-on seized the Persian baggage and treasure at Damascus. About eight thousand Greek mercenaries escaped with their commanders, among them A-min-tas and Thy-mon-das, says Arrian.

The letters. Darius wrote to Alexander asking for his family back, and offering friendship. In Arrian's version, he said Alexander had invaded without any wrong done to him. Alexander answered that he came to avenge Persia's wrongs against the Greeks, and demanded to be recognised as lord of Asia. These letters come to us in the writers' own versions, which differ. They are not surviving originals.

The road to Tyre. Alexander did not chase Darius inland. He marched south along the coast, taking the harbours of the Persian fleet. Ar-a-dus, Bib-los and Sidon submitted. Tyre refused his request to enter the island city to sacrifice. Alexander began a siege, which Plutarch and Dye-o-dor-us say lasted seven months. Our page on the Siege of Tyre tells that story. Darius was still free, and the empire could still raise another army. The two kings would meet again at Gaw-ga-mee-la, in 331 BCE.

At the Gran-eye-kus in 334 BCE, Alexander defeated the Persian Say-traps' cavalry and their Greek mercenaries, and opened western Anatolia. At Issus in 333 BCE, he defeated Darius the Third. Darius escaped; his family was captured. Neither battle ended the Persian Empire. How the Gran-eye-kus began: an attack at once, in Arrian; a dawn crossing, in Dye-o-dor-us. Who struck whom in the fight at the bank. The sizes of the armies and the numbers killed: the Persian totals are far too large to be counts. Where exactly the two battles were fought. No Persian history of these battles survives. We see Darius almost only through Greek and Roman eyes.
